---
title: "7.3 Methodology and alternatives"
order: 3
---

Early Warning is three components served side by side. A gradient-boosted model estimates
each account's probability of deterioration; two cutoffs, set once at training, turn that
probability into a tier; and a set of fixed rules, which are not fitted to anything, name
the warning signs present on the account. They are described here in the order the code
builds them.

## The model: LightGBM

A gradient-boosted tree ensemble, fitted on the {{< var ews.n_train >}} training accounts
([7.2](data.qmd#ews-split)) with fixed hyperparameters and the platform seed:

```python
model = LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31,   # ews/src/train.py
                       subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, random_state=SEED,
                       n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, categorical_feature=EWS_CATEGORICAL)
```

The hyperparameters are constants, not the result of a search; there is no early stopping
and no validation set. The probability is `predict_proba`'s, uncalibrated: no Platt or
isotonic step follows the fit.

With {{< var ews.model.n_estimators >}} trees of up to {{< var ews.model.num_leaves >}} leaves
on {{< var ews.n_train >}} rows and a noisy label, the model **fits its training rows almost
perfectly**: training AUC {{< var ews.train.auc >}}, against {{< var ews.auc >}} on the
held-out accounts ([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-held-out-vs-whole-book)). That gap does not
make the held-out figures wrong — they are measured on rows the trees never saw — but it
matters wherever the model scores its own training rows, which is most of the book. It
drives findings 1 and 2 ([7.7](limitations.qmd)).

### What the model uses {#ews-importance}

LightGBM's own importances, from the saved booster: *gain* is how much each feature's splits
reduced the loss, *split* is how often it was used.

{{< include ../../_generated/ews-importance.md >}}

No feature dominates. `pd_score` ranks {{< var ews.importance.gain.pd_score_rank >}}th of
{{< var ews.n_features >}} by gain and {{< var ews.importance.split.pd_score_rank >}}th by
split count; with `business_score` the scorecard's two columns carry
{{< var ews.importance.score_gain_share >}} of the gain.

Read that with care. Importance describes how the fitted trees spread their splits, and a
model that fits its training rows almost perfectly spreads them over many features. It does
not say what the model would lose without a feature. The benchmark does: ranked by
`pd_score` alone, the held-out accounts come out about as well as the model ranks them
([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-benchmark)). Low importance for the score and a benchmark the
model cannot beat are consistent with the behavioural features re-learning, through
correlated columns, much of what the score already knows. That is a reading of the two
measurements, not a decomposition.

## Risk tiers, calibrated at training {#ews-tiers}

After fitting, `train.py` sets the two tier cutoffs as quantiles of the model's probability
over **all** {{< var ews.n_book >}} booked accounts — training and held-out rows together —
and writes them into `metadata.json`:

```python
prob_full = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]                    # ews/src/train.py
tiers = dict(EWS_TIERS)
tiers["t_high"] = float(round(np.quantile(prob_full, 0.90), 4))
tiers["t_med"] = float(round(np.quantile(prob_full, 0.70), 4))
```

The committed cutoffs are `t_high` = {{< var ews.t_high >}} and `t_med` =
{{< var ews.t_med >}}. They replace the seed values in `shared.config.EWS_TIERS`, which are
placeholders. `risk_tier` then reads them:

```python
def risk_tier(prob, tiers: dict) -> str:                     # ews/src/watchlist.py
    if prob >= tiers["t_high"]:
        return "High"
    if prob >= tiers["t_med"]:
        return "Medium"
    return "Low"
```

By construction, then, the book splits {{< var ews.tier.High.share >}} High,
{{< var ews.tier.Medium.share >}} Medium and {{< var ews.tier.Low.share >}} Low
({{< var ews.tier.High.n >}}, {{< var ews.tier.Medium.n >}} and {{< var ews.tier.Low.n >}}
accounts). The cutoffs are positions in the probability distribution, not risk limits: what
is fixed is the review workload ([7.4](assumptions.qmd#ews-tiers-as-a-fixed-mix)). Because
{{< var ews.n_train >}} of the {{< var ews.n_book >}} probabilities they are taken over are
in-sample, the mix on accounts the model has not seen is very different — finding 1
([7.7](limitations.qmd)).

## Named triggers {#ews-triggers}

`flag_triggers` (`ews/src/triggers.py`) is a rule layer beside the model, not inside it. Each
rule compares one behavioural feature with a threshold from `shared.config.EWS_TRIGGERS`; an
account carries the name of every rule that fires:

```python
rules = [                                                   # ews/src/triggers.py
    ("HIGH_UTILIZATION", util_recent > cfg["high_utilization"]),
    ("RISING_UTILIZATION", util_drift > cfg["rising_utilization"]),
    ("DELINQUENCY", (dpd_max >= cfg["dpd_severe"]) | (dpd_recent > 0)),
    ("DEPOSIT_DECLINE", deposit_decline > cfg["deposit_decline"]),
    ("FREQUENT_OVERDRAFTS", overdraft_recent >= cfg["overdraft_recent"]),
]
```

| Trigger | Rule | Threshold | Source of the threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| `{{< var ews.trigger.high_utilization.name >}}` | `util_recent >` | {{< var ews.trigger.high_utilization.clause.util_recent.threshold >}} | `EWS_TRIGGERS["{{< var ews.trigger.high_utilization.clause.util_recent.config_key >}}"]` |
| `{{< var ews.trigger.rising_utilization.name >}}` | `util_drift >` | {{< var ews.trigger.rising_utilization.clause.util_drift.threshold >}} | `EWS_TRIGGERS["{{< var ews.trigger.rising_utilization.clause.util_drift.config_key >}}"]` |
| `{{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.name >}}` | `dpd_max >=` | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_max.threshold >}} | `EWS_TRIGGERS["{{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_max.config_key >}}"]` |
| | *or* `dpd_recent >` | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_recent.threshold >}} | {{< var ews.trigger.delinquency.clause.dpd_recent.config_key >}}, in `triggers.py` |
| `{{< var ews.trigger.deposit_decline.name >}}` | `deposit_decline_pct >` | {{< var ews.trigger.deposit_decline.clause.deposit_decline_pct.threshold >}} | `EWS_TRIGGERS["{{< var ews.trigger.deposit_decline.clause.deposit_decline_pct.config_key >}}"]` |
| `{{< var ews.trigger.frequent_overdrafts.name >}}` | `overdraft_recent >=` | {{< var ews.trigger.frequent_overdrafts.clause.overdraft_recent.threshold >}} | `EWS_TRIGGERS["{{< var ews.trigger.frequent_overdrafts.clause.overdraft_recent.config_key >}}"]` |

The thresholds are policy values, not estimates: none was set from this book's
distribution ([7.4](assumptions.qmd#ews-trigger-thresholds-are-generic)). `DELINQUENCY` is the
only compound rule, and its second clause has a threshold written into the code rather than
the configuration. On this data the configured clause never fires and the hard-coded one
does all the work — finding 6 ([7.7](limitations.qmd)). How often each trigger fires, and how
well, is in [7.5](performance.qmd#ews-trigger-performance).

## Why both: a probability and a reason

The model and the triggers answer different questions, and neither consults the other:

- **The tier ranks.** It uses every feature at once, including the score, and it is the
  part the gate measures ([7.9](gate.qmd)). It cannot say what is wrong with an account;
  its SHAP reasons are an attribution, and a reason like "the score" is not one a
  relationship manager can raise with a customer.
- **The triggers explain.** Each names one observable fact about the account in the
  customer's own terms — utilisation, a late payment, falling deposits — and turns a
  probability into a conversation. They are exact, auditable and stable, and they do not
  depend on a retrain.

The cost of keeping them independent is that they can disagree: a High-tier account can carry
no trigger, and most triggered accounts are not High ([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-tiers-and-triggers)).
The design treats that as information for the reviewer, not as an error; whether the triggers
carry enough signal to be worth the reviewer's attention is finding 7.

## Why a gradient-boosted model {#ews-why-lightgbm}

Monitoring is a different problem from origination: the features are trends and counts over
time, their effects plausibly have thresholds (utilisation that matters only near the limit,
a first late payment), and the output prioritises a review rather than deciding credit. A
flexible learner that finds thresholds and interactions without hand-binning fits that
problem, and a monitoring model's lower risk rating (Tier 2, [D0](../d0-summary.qmd#risk-tiering)) makes
the loss of an exact decomposition more tolerable than at origination. The choice was made at development and is recorded here
so it can be challenged.

What the evidence says about it, from [7.5](performance.qmd):

- **There is little left to find.** On the held-out accounts the model ranks within a
  whisker of the strongest model the observable columns support
  ([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-ceiling)). A different learner on the same columns would not do
  much better.
- **It is not distinguishable from the score it consumes.** On AUC, the paired interval for
  the model's lead over `pd_score` alone contains zero
  ([7.5](performance.qmd#ews-benchmark)). What it does do that the score alone does not is
  clear the capture gate: `pd_score` alone captures {{< var ews.pd_score.capture >}} in its
  top decile, below the {{< var ews.gate.capture_min >}} gate — one measurement, without an
  interval for the difference.

### Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Status | What it would and would not give |
|---|---|---|
| Rank the book by the scorecard's `pd_score` alone | measured, not adopted | Nearly the same AUC on the held-out accounts, and no model to maintain; but it misses the capture gate on this sample, and it would never react to behaviour after booking (finding 4). |
| A logistic or scorecard-style model on the panel features | not built | Exact reason codes, as D4 has, and far less room to memorise the training rows; whether it would rank as well is unmeasured. |
| Triggers alone, without a model | measured as part of [7.5](performance.qmd#ews-trigger-performance), not adopted | Exact reasons, but on this book the triggers fire on most accounts and barely beat the base rate (finding 7). |

None has been rejected on evidence that it ranks worse. The open question — whether the
behavioural layer adds enough over the score to justify a model — is carried to the next
redevelopment by finding 4 ([7.8](monitoring.qmd#ews-redevelopment-triggers)).

## Reason codes: SHAP {#ews-why-shap}

A tree ensemble has no exact decomposition into per-feature points the way the scorecard
does (D4.3), so the model's reasons, where they are served, come from SHAP, as in
adjudication ([D5.3](../adjudication/methodology.qmd#adj-reason-codes)). `score_population`
runs `shap.TreeExplainer` over every booked account and keeps each account's top three
adverse features with `top_adverse_shap`; the v1 account endpoint and the v2 workbench serve
them. `train.py` runs the same explainer on a few held-out rows as a sanity check only;
nothing is gated on it.

They are served because a tier with no reason is not actionable, and the triggers do not
always supply one. SHAP carries D5's caveats: it is an attribution method with its own
choices, it splits credit between correlated features (here the scorecard's two columns, and
the utilisation measures among themselves), and a reason that is the score is a model output,
not a fact about the business. Where a trigger fired, the trigger is the reason to give;
the SHAP reasons explain the probability.

## Feature selection

None, in the sense of a search: `EWS_FEATURE_COLUMNS` is a fixed list
([7.2](data.qmd#ews-features)). `colsample_bytree` draws a random subset of the columns for
each tree, which is regularisation, not selection.
